slides.text: At the Kurud village, caste Hindus opened the temple doors to Harijans in Gandhi's presence. A door closed for centuries, opened in one afternoon. Gandhi stood as witness as the community chose to open it themselves.
slides.visualDescription: Title card: Ancient temple doors in Kurud village — heavy wood and iron — slowly opening. Harijan families standing at the threshold for the first time. Gandhi watching as witness. Light pouring from the interior. The most important door in Chhattisgarh opening.

slides.text: November 22-23, 1933. Gandhi in Raipur. His central purpose: untouchability. He visited the Baithd School at Shanichari Bazar in Durg — the integrated school where since 1926, children of upper castes and Harijans sat together on the same sackcloth.
slides.visualDescription: The Baithd School, Durg — children of all castes sitting together on the same simple sackcloth. Upper caste children and Harijan children shoulder to shoulder. Gandhi walking through the classroom, face transformed by what he sees. What should be normal, made real.

slides.text: Ghanshyam Singh Gupta had told Gandhi about the Baithd School. When Gandhi arrived and saw children of all castes learning together since 1926 — seven years before his visit — he understood that Chhattisgarh had been doing this work without him.
slides.visualDescription: Ghanshyam Singh Gupta presenting the Baithd School to Gandhi. The story: since 1926, upper caste and Harijan children together. Seven years of this. Gandhi arriving to find a revolution already underway. His admiration visible. Chhattisgarh again ahead of the script.

slides.text: Gandhi had food while sitting with the children of the untouchable class at Baithd School. Not as performance — as practice. He ate with them as equals. The Mahatma eating beside children who were told they polluted the spaces they occupied.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi seated on the floor of Baithd School eating alongside Harijan children. Simple food. The sackcloth under them both. The children at first uncertain, then settling into the normality of eating with someone who respects them. Dignity made edible.

slides.text: The school principal — who had built this integrated institution in 1926, three years before Gandhi's Salt March, seven years before his Harijan tour — was proof that the ideas Gandhi championed were not his alone. They were alive wherever there was courage.
slides.visualDescription: The school principal standing beside Gandhi at the Baithd School — the man who built this before Gandhi made it a national cause. Two people who had the same idea independently, meeting now in the place where the idea had been built into walls and curriculum.

slides.text: From the school, Gandhi went to the meetings of upper-caste Hindus in Raipur. His message: untouchability is not Hinduism. It is a cancer that must be cut out. The Vedas do not endorse it. God does not endorse it. You are endorsing it by your silence.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi addressing upper-caste Hindus in Raipur — not the usual admiring crowd but people being challenged. His message firm but not angry: untouchability is not your religion. Your silence is its endorsement. The hall uncomfortable. The truth heard anyway.

slides.text: Gandhi's argument against untouchability was always theological as well as moral: he believed that God lives in every human being. To treat a person as untouchable is to treat God as untouchable. The theological argument made to a deeply religious people.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi making his theological argument — speaking to a religious gathering in Raipur. His words: God lives in every human being. To touch a Harijan is to touch God. To refuse to touch them is to refuse God. The sacred argument for equality. Deeply Hindu logic.

slides.text: The Satnami community of Chhattisgarh — followers of the Satnam faith founded by Ghasidas — had rejected caste from their beginning. Their very name means 'those who take the true name.' Gandhi visited their communities and found fellow travellers.
slides.visualDescription: The Satnami community of Chhattisgarh — their distinctive white dress, their refusal of caste. Gandhi meeting Satnami leaders, recognising in their faith the anti-untouchability values he was trying to build into the Congress. Fellow travellers, different roads.

slides.text: The Satnam Ashram of Pt. Sundarlal Sharma — built as a community of equals where Satnami people were full members — was Gandhi's most powerful evidence in Chhattisgarh that his vision was achievable. It had already been achieved. Here. In this district.
slides.visualDescription: The Satnam Ashram — peaceful, functioning, beautiful in its equality. Gandhi walking through it with the expression of a man seeing his theory made real. The ashram as the proof. Pt. Sharma's decades of work standing before Gandhi as architecture.

slides.text: 'Harijan Uddhar mein aap mere bhi guru hain.' In the Satnam Ashram, Gandhi said this to Pt. Sundarlal Sharma. You are even my Guru in the salvation of Harijans. The Mahatma calling a Chhattisgarhi reformer his teacher. The moment of highest recognition.
slides.visualDescription: The moment at the Satnam Ashram: Gandhi facing Sharma, hands on his shoulders, making the declaration. Harijan Uddhar mein aap mere bhi guru hain. Sharma's face — the emotion of a lifetime of work being seen and named by the one person who truly understands its value.

slides.text: The Victoria Garden meeting in Raipur — November 23, 1933. The largest gathering of the second visit. One lakh people. One hundred thousand. The biggest crowd that Raipur had ever seen, assembled to hear Gandhi speak about human dignity.
slides.visualDescription: Victoria Garden, Raipur, November 23, 1933. One lakh people — the garden invisible beneath them. A sea of humanity as far as the eye can see. Gandhi on the stage, small against the enormity of the crowd. One voice speaking about dignity to one hundred thousand.

slides.text: Gandhi spoke for over an hour at Victoria Garden. His subject: untouchability as the greatest blot on Hinduism. His argument: if we want freedom from the British, we must first free our own Harijans. External and internal freedom are one.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi at the Victoria Garden podium — the one-lakh crowd before him. His words: freedom from the British and freedom for the Harijans are one movement. You cannot ask to be treated as a full human being while denying it to another. The logical unity of freedom.

slides.text: At Victoria Garden, Makhan the barber came to cut Gandhi's hair. He was a Harijan — and he hesitated, knowing that his touch was considered polluting. Gandhi called him forward. He cut Gandhi's hair. The Mahatma's head in the hands of the untouchable.
slides.visualDescription: Makhan the barber at Victoria Garden — hesitating before Gandhi. Gandhi's gesture of invitation: come, cut my hair. Makhan's hands, trembling, beginning. Gandhi's head in the hands that India called untouchable. One hundred thousand people witnessing this.

slides.text: After cutting Gandhi's hair, Makhan asked for one thing: to touch Gandhi's feet. Gandhi let him. Then Gandhi offered Makhan a rupee — and Makhan would not spend it. He kept it as a sacred object for the rest of his life.
slides.visualDescription: Makhan touching Gandhi's feet — the reverse of expected hierarchy. Gandhi receiving the touch. Then Gandhi giving Makhan a rupee. Makhan holding it with both hands as if it is gold. The rupee that he will never spend — kept as the most precious thing he will ever own.

slides.text: Makhan's kept rupee — never spent. A simple coin that became a shrine object, passed through his family as the most sacred possession. The rupee that represents: I was seen. I was honoured. I was touched by the Mahatma and I touched him back.
slides.visualDescription: The rupee in close-up — small, ordinary, colonial-era coin. Makhan's hands cradling it. His face: the expression of a man who has received the most important recognition of his life from the most important person of his age. A coin worth everything.

slides.text: An old woman at a Raipur meeting asked Gandhi: 'Let me wash your feet.' Gandhi agreed. She washed them. She then drank the water — the foot-washing water as sacred as temple water. Her faith absolute and complete and, in Gandhi's view, not to be refused.
slides.visualDescription: An elder woman at a Raipur meeting, asking to wash Gandhi's feet. Gandhi seated, allowing it. She washing with devotion. Then drinking the water. Gandhi watching with mixed emotions — moved by her faith, concerned about the deification. His compassion winning.

slides.text: Gandhi consistently pushed back against being worshipped — he was not God, he insisted, and the Harijan cause required not worship of him but practical action. But he did not always win this argument with the people of Chhattisgarh who loved him.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi at a Raipur meeting, gently but firmly trying to redirect devotion into action. The crowd's love flowing toward him. His effort to channel it away from himself and toward the cause. The impossible task of a saint who does not want to be a saint.

slides.text: Meera Ben — Madelaine Slade, the English aristocrat who had become Gandhi's disciple and companion — was present throughout the second visit. Her presence: an English woman in service of the freedom of India, the irony made into an argument.
slides.visualDescription: Meera Ben — Madelaine Slade, dressed in Indian sari, hair simply arranged — beside Gandhi in Raipur. An English woman who chose India over England, who chose Gandhi's mission over her class. Her presence as its own argument against colonial hierarchy.

slides.text: Mahadev Desai — Gandhi's secretary, biographer, constant companion — recorded everything of the second visit in his meticulous notes. His diary the closest thing we have to a continuous record of what Gandhi said and did in Chhattisgarh in 1933.
slides.visualDescription: Mahadev Desai writing in his diary beside Gandhi — capturing every meeting, every speech, every interaction. His pen moving constantly. The future historians' source sitting at Gandhi's right hand, recording what would otherwise be lost. Memory preserved in ink.

slides.text: Thakkar Bapa — Amritlal Vithaldas Thakkar — the man who had devoted his life to tribal welfare, traveled with Gandhi through Chhattisgarh specifically to advance the Harijan cause. Two men with one mission moving through the land together.
slides.visualDescription: Thakkar Bapa traveling with Gandhi through Chhattisgarh — two men in the same motor, the same purpose. Thakkar Bapa's life work in tribal welfare making him the perfect companion for Gandhi's Harijan tour. Two missions meeting in one journey.

slides.text: The Harijan Sevak Sangh — the organisation Gandhi founded to support Harijan uplift — collected funds throughout the second visit. The Tilak Fund of 1920 had supported political independence. The Harijan Fund of 1933 supported social independence.
slides.visualDescription: The Harijan Sevak Sangh fund being collected in Raipur — people donating to the cause of Harijan uplift. The fund bag filling as the Tilak Fund bag had filled thirteen years before. The progression from political to social freedom marked by a change of funds.

slides.text: Temples that had been closed to Harijans for generations opened their doors during Gandhi's Chhattisgarh visit. Not all — some stayed closed, and Gandhi noted this with sadness. But the ones that opened: proof that one man's presence could accelerate centuries of change.
slides.visualDescription: A sequence of temple doors — some opening during Gandhi's visit, some staying closed. The contrast: the open door with its light and the closed door with its shadow. Gandhi acknowledging both — the progress and the persistence. The work ongoing even as he witnesses it.

slides.text: The night procession of November 22 — from Amapara to Budhapara, Raipur. Three hours for a short distance. Aarti at every step, flowers, lamps. A city expressing its love for a man who would not let it love him more than it loved its own Harijans.
slides.visualDescription: The night procession — torches, aarti flames, flower petals, lamps lining the road. Gandhi moving slowly through three hours of devotion. At every house: a lamp. At every corner: aarti. The city pouring itself out. Gandhi accepting and redirecting simultaneously.

slides.text: The Raipur of 1933 was different from the Raipur of 1920. The Raipur District Congress Committee — founded in 1920 — had grown into a fully functioning organisation. The leaders were older, more experienced. The movement was deeper. The ground was richer.
slides.visualDescription: Raipur 1933 compared with 1920 — the same streets but transformed. The DCC building instead of a temporary tent. Experienced leaders instead of newly organised ones. The movement thirteen years mature. The soil that had been freshly turned now rich and productive.

slides.text: Ravi Shankar Shukla — first DCC secretary 1920, now a senior leader of the Central Province Congress — received Gandhi at his home, Shukla Niwas, in 1933. The same man, thirteen years of leadership later. The continuity of Chhattisgarh's commitment made visible.
slides.visualDescription: Ravi Shankar Shukla in 1933 — older, more lined, carrying the weight of thirteen years of movement leadership. Receiving Gandhi at Shukla Niwas. The same man who signed the DCC papers in 1920. The continuity of a person who chose and stayed with the choice.

slides.text: The door at the Kurud temple opened. The door at the Baithd School had been open since 1926. The door of Pt. Sharma's Satnam Ashram had been open for decades. Chhattisgarh had been opening doors before Gandhi came to open them.
slides.visualDescription: A visual sequence of open doors: the Baithd School since 1926, the Satnam Ashram for decades, the Kurud temple in 1933. Each door a different year, the same opening. Chhattisgarh as a province that had been ahead of the national curve on this issue.

slides.text: But some doors stayed closed. Gandhi noted this. The movement against untouchability in Chhattisgarh was real and substantial — but it was not complete. Gandhi's visit accelerated it. It did not finish it. That work would continue long after 1933.
slides.visualDescription: The closed doors — temples that did not open in 1933. Gandhi looking at them. Noting. Not judging the people, but naming the fact. The movement incomplete. The work continuing. The visit not the end but a powerful push along an ongoing road.

slides.text: The Mahatma at the door — both metaphor and fact. Gandhi standing before the doors of India's oldest injustice, asking them to open. Sometimes they opened. Sometimes they did not. He kept standing. He kept asking. He kept coming back.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi standing before a closed temple door — his hand raised, not in command but in request. The door not yet opening. His posture: patient, permanent, not going anywhere. The Mahatma at the door as a posture of lifelong commitment. Standing as the act itself.

slides.text: The Harijan children of Raipur who met Gandhi in 1933 — who ate beside him, whose hair he touched — carried that memory. Their children's children carry it still. Not as political memory but as personal memory: he came to us, he sat with us, he was not afraid of us.
slides.visualDescription: Harijan children of Raipur in 1933 meeting Gandhi. Their eyes: open, wondering, disbelieving. Gandhi at their level — seated with them. The memory of this moment passing through generations as the most precious inheritance. He came to us. He was not afraid.

slides.text: Makhan's rupee — kept, never spent, passed through his family as the most sacred possession. A rupee that Gandhi gave to a barber he honoured by receiving a haircut from. The economics of dignity: a coin worth everything because of what it meant.
slides.visualDescription: Makhan's rupee in present-day hands — a descendant holding it. The coin unchanged but carrying generations of meaning. Simple metal transformed by one afternoon in Victoria Garden into the most valuable object a Harijan barber's family has ever owned.

slides.text: The old woman who washed Gandhi's feet and drank the water. Her faith: absolute. Gandhi's response: acceptance. Not the acceptance of a god receiving worship, but the acceptance of a human being who understands what this moment means to another human being.
slides.visualDescription: The elder woman with her hands still wet from washing Gandhi's feet. Her face: complete, satisfied, at peace. Having done the most important thing she will ever do. Gandhi's face beside hers: the face of a man who has received something he cannot repay.

slides.text: The Mahatma at the door of caste. Of temples. Of schools. Of barbershops. Of kitchens. Of every institution that maintained untouchability. Knocking. Not with violence. With presence. With presence that said: this door will open, and when it does, I will be here.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi at multiple doors simultaneously — temple, school, kitchen, barbershop. Each door a different form of the same barrier. His presence at each: patient, permanent, irresistible. The door as the central image of the second visit. Closed. Being opened. Opened.

slides.text: What Chhattisgarh gave Gandhi in the second visit: the proof that his mission had already taken root here before he arrived. The Baithd School since 1926. Pt. Sharma's decades of work. The Satnam community. Chhattisgarh, again, ahead of the script.
slides.visualDescription: Chhattisgarh's anti-untouchability work laid out chronologically: Sharma's Janeu movement 1910s, Satnam Ashram 1920s, Baithd School 1926, Tamora Satyagraha solidarity 1930. All before Gandhi's 1933 Harijan tour. A province that led its own reform.

slides.text: What Gandhi gave Chhattisgarh in the second visit: the national scale, the formal acknowledgement, the Harijan Sevak Sangh resources, and his own body — eating with Harijan children, receiving a haircut from a Harijan barber — as the most powerful argument.
slides.visualDescription: What Gandhi contributed to Chhattisgarh's anti-untouchability work: the national scale, the Harijan Sevak Sangh resources, and most importantly his own body as argument — eating, being touched, touching. The body as the most powerful platform for the message.

slides.text: The exchange was complete. Chhattisgarh gave Gandhi proof. Gandhi gave Chhattisgarh scale. Pt. Sharma gave Gandhi a guru's precedent. Gandhi gave Sharma his public recognition. The second visit as a complete exchange of gifts between equals.
slides.visualDescription: The exchange of the second visit visualised as a two-way flow: from Chhattisgarh to Gandhi (proof, precedent, courage), from Gandhi to Chhattisgarh (scale, recognition, resources). Not a visit of the great man to the grateful province. A meeting of equals.

slides.text: November 23, 1933. The Victoria Garden meeting ends. One lakh people disperse slowly. Makhan carries his rupee home. The woman who washed Gandhi's feet is still sitting, hands folded, at peace. The Mahatma moves on to Bilaspur.
slides.visualDescription: The end of the Victoria Garden meeting — the one lakh dispersing slowly, reluctantly. Makhan walking home with his rupee held carefully. The elder woman still seated, at peace. Gandhi's motor departing for Bilaspur. Raipur transforming in its wake.

slides.text: One lakh at Victoria Garden. A barber's kept rupee. An old woman's foot-washing water. A temple door in Kurud. The Mahatma's presence made permanent in objects and acts and memories. Next: Episode 4 — The Promise at Bilaspur.
slides.visualDescription: A final image collage from the second visit so far: Victoria Garden crowd, Makhan's rupee, the Kurud temple door, the foot-washing elder. Each image carrying its complete meaning. Title card: Episode 4 — The Promise at Bilaspur.
